paragraphs: It is not enough for the assembled people to have once fixed the constitution of the State by approving a body of law; it is not enough for it to have set up a perpetual government, or to have provided once and for all for the election of magistrates. Besides the extraordinary assemblies that unforeseen circumstances may require, there must be fixed periodic assemblies that cannot be abolished or postponed, so that on the proper day the people is lawfully called together by law, without any need for a formal summons.

But apart from these assemblies that are authorized by their date alone, any assembly of the people that the appointed magistrates have not summoned, in the prescribed forms, should be regarded as unlawful, and everything it does as null and void, because the order to assemble should itself come from the law.

How often lawful assemblies should be held depends on so many considerations that no exact rules can be given. It can only be said in general that the stronger the government, the more often the Sovereign should show itself.

This, I shall be told, may do for a single city; but what is to be done when the State has several? Should the sovereign authority be divided? Or should it be concentrated in one city, with all the others made subject to it?

Neither, I reply. First, the sovereign authority is one and simple, and cannot be divided without being destroyed. In the second place, one city cannot legitimately be made subject to another, any more than one nation can, because the essence of the body politic lies in the reconciliation of obedience and liberty, and the words subject and Sovereign are identical correlatives, whose meaning is joined in the single word “citizen.”

I answer further that uniting several cities into one city is always bad, and that anyone who wants such a union should not expect to escape its natural disadvantages. It is pointless to raise the abuses of great States against someone who wants only small ones. But how can small States be given the strength to resist great ones, as the Greek cities once resisted the Great King, and as Holland and Switzerland more recently resisted the House of Austria?

Nevertheless, if the State cannot be reduced to its right size, one resource still remains: to allow no capital, to make the seat of government move from city to city, and to have the Provincial Estates of the country meet in each city in turn.

Populate the territory evenly, extend the same rights everywhere, carry abundance and life to every part of it: by these means the State will become as strong and as well governed as possible. Remember that the walls of cities are built from the ruins of the houses of the countryside. For every palace I see rise in the capital, I see in my mind’s eye a whole country made desolate.
